messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Certain Songs: Certain songs, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Vignette:
Dmitri Volkov is a 56-year-old European-American professional dancer and choreographer who presented for psychological assessment following a motor vehicle accident that occurred approximately fourteen months ago, in which a pedestrian was critically injured. He is married and continues to work in the performing arts, though his relationship to that work has changed in ways he describes as irreversible.

The incident took place on a Saturday evening in late autumn. Dmitri had been driving home after a rehearsal that had run long, navigating a stretch of road he knew well, near the arts district where his company is based. A woman stepped from between parked cars into his lane. He braked, but not in time. The impact was low-speed but sufficient to throw her to the ground with a fractured pelvis and a traumatic brain injury that left her hospitalised for several weeks. Dmitri remained at the scene, knelt beside her in the road, held her hand while sirens approached. He remembers the particular song that had been playing on the car radio — a slow, orchestral piece he had loved for years — still audible through the open door as emergency responders arrived. He was not charged with any offence. The investigation concluded that the pedestrian had been concealed by parked vehicles and that Dmitri had been driving within the speed limit. None of this has mattered to him.

In the weeks that followed, Dmitri found himself replaying the moment of impact with an involuntary precision that felt nothing like ordinary memory. Images of the car striking her body arrived without warning, summoned by nothing he could predict and resisted by nothing he could do. He began to notice that certain songs — particularly anything orchestral or slow in tempo — could pull him back to that roadside with a vividness that left him gripping whatever surface was nearest. He came to understand these moments not as flashbacks in any clinical sense he had words for, but as proof that something in him had been permanently rearranged. He had come to believe, with a certainty that resisted all counter-argument, that he had failed in the most fundamental obligation a person can carry: the protection of someone vulnerable. That she had stepped unexpectedly from between parked cars was, in his accounting, beside the point. He had been behind the wheel. He had not stopped in time.

His avoidance of the street where the accident occurred became absolute within the first month. He reroutes every journey to ensure he never passes through that part of the arts district, which means he now enters and leaves his own rehearsal studio by a longer, less convenient route. His colleagues have noticed. He has offered no explanation. He also began working to keep the event out of his mind whenever it surfaced during the day, pushing against the images with a concentrated effort that leaves him exhausted by evening. He dwells instead on who he was before that Saturday — a man who moved through the world with physical confidence and a sense of creative authority — and finds the comparison unbearable. He has not been able to teach the way he once did. In crowded rehearsal spaces, when bodies press close and the noise of a full company rises, he finds himself unable to track what is happening around him, his attention fracturing, his body braced for something he cannot name. Several dancers have commented that he seems distracted or short-tempered. One junior choreographer he had been mentoring has quietly stepped back from the relationship.

At home, he lies awake long after his wife has fallen asleep, unable to surrender the vigilance he feels he owes to the night. He cannot relax even in rooms he knows to be safe. He will never forgive himself for not doing more, he told his assessor in the first session — not a figure of speech, but a statement of settled conviction. What finally brought him to seek help was his wife's quiet observation that she had lost him, and that she did not know where he had gone. What he fears most, sitting across from a clinician for the first time, is that she is right.
